messages.subject: Assumptions of random distributions
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I recently came across the following PhD thesis which has some
interesting information about the distributrions of animals and line
transect sampling biases:

J.L. Cooke (1993) Assessing populations in complex systems. PhD thesis,
Texas A&M University.

In this work he modelled various distributions of animals - regular to
clumped and placed transects of different sizes on these distributions
using a stratified random sampling approach. He finds that there are
several biases that occur depending on the size of transects and the
spacing of animals. For instance if  he concludes that if animal spacing
is greater than 10-15 times the transect width then you will tend to
obtain overestimates of populations. With more clumped distributions you
tend to overestimate population density and even distributions tend to
underestimate density.

I have been involved with primate censusing in Africa and one of the
general findings where studies have compared line transect estimates of
primate densities with 'known' values from habituated groups within the
census area is that primate densities are overestimated by line
transects. (this would fit with the bias quoted above where primate
groups are usually spaced by more than 10 times transect width). The
solution proposed by some is to use observer-animal distance to
calculate the distance at which sighting of primate groups drops off
rather than the perpendicular distance. To me this makes no sense as it
is the perpendicular distance which is important because as you move
forward animals that are far in front of you will be seen if close to
the line but if far from the line they may be missed. This proposed
solution only works because it reduces the density estimate but as far
as I can see it has no validity as a method and there is no mathematical
basis for using it.

The thesis by Cooke proposes a method to correct the bias but I am not
competent to judge this and was wondering whether anyone else has looked
at this issue. What confuses me most is that in the Buckland et al
(1993) Bible it is stated that the 'distribution of animals does not
have to be random - only the placement of transects with respect to the
animals' - yet Cooke comes to the conclusion that this is not the case.
Can anyone help me on this?

Andy Plumptre

messages.subject: Re: Assumptions of random distributions
messages.body_plain:
I have not seen the thesis.  There is nothing mathematically to back up
the reported findings.  Whether animals are clustered or distributed
evenly, if lines are randomly located (or a grid of lines randomly
superimposed) on the study area, and if other assumptions hold, then
estimation of animal density will be approximately unbiased.  I suspect
therefore, if the thesis is reported accurately, that it has some flaw.
What was the magnitude of the bias?  Did the bias differ significantly
from zero?

Radial distance models were once quite popular, but were shown some years
ago not to be robust to failures of their unrealistic assumptions.  To
record radial distances and analyse them as if they were perpendicular
distances would not only be silly but also lead to models that simply
don't fit the data.

If there is upward bias in surveys of ape populations of known size, it is
likely to be due to some more obvious failure of assumption.  e.g.
'random' animal movement leads to upward bias, which can be appreciable if
average speed is around half the speed of the observer or more.  Also,
undetected responsive movement towards the observer causes upward bias.
There is an 'accepted' procedure amongst some of the 'ape' community that
generates substantial upward bias - distances are measured to the nearest
member of a group, or possibly to the first member of the group detected,
which tends to be one of the nearer ones.  This gives a perpendicular
distance that is too small, and leads to upward bias in the estimates.
Ideally, the observer should measure to the 'centre of gravity' of the
group.  If this is difficult because members of the group are too spread
out, record the distance to each individual animal.  The centre of
gravity can then be calculated later - and in fact, it might be better to
enter each individual distance into the analysis, as if these were
separate animals rather than a single group, if the group is well spread
out.  Contrary to the reported conclusions of the thesis, Distance
actually gives very reliable estimates, even with such extreme clustering
of the distances and violation of the assumption of independence, provided
the number of groups detected is reasonably large.

Steve Buckland
